Puka Nacua Has Been a Key Target for Matthew Stafford

Despite missing time earlier in the season with a groin/hip issue, Nacua has been Matthew Stafford's most reliable receiving option when healthy.

In four games, the wide receiver has recorded 37 receptions for 417 yards and one touchdown. He has an 81.8 PFN WR Impact Grade , which ranks 15th among wide receivers.

If Nacua is unavailable against the Raiders, receiver Konata Mumpfield could be asked to take on a bigger role.

The Rams face an urgent must-win scenario against Las Vegas to prevent their season from spiraling out of reach, but this spate of injuries could test Sean McVay's resolve.

articles.title: Texas' make-or-break moment arrives for Steve Sarkisian, Arch Manning
articles.summary: The Longhorns' season has devolved into a soap opera and the College Football Playoff is slipping away. Can they solve their problems against Ole Miss before...
articles.body:
Texas coach Steve Sarkisian used the "rearview mirror-windshield" analogy at his press conference Tuesday to describe the last two weeks.

It's about what lies ahead for No. 19 Texas (4-2, 1-2 SEC) against No. 7 Ole Miss (5-1, 3-1 SEC). The Longhorns and Rebels meet at 7:30 p.m. ET in the "Saturday Night Football" spotlight game on ABC at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium.

The rear view shows back-to-back losses to Oklahoma and Florida that have dropped Texas from No. 1 in the AP Poll — 18 spots in two weeks. The Rebels are in front now, and a loss here would be much harder to leave behind for Sarkisian, quarterback Arch Manning, edge rusher Colin Simmons and the Longhorns as a whole.

"The key to the drill for us moving forward is we have to have constructive conversations," Sarkisian said at a press conference Monday . "We've had those. It's easy to listen to the outside noise and the sky is falling and the season is over. What are we going to do next year? Hey, man we're 4-2. Let's be part of the solution. Let's go 1-0 this week and let's get to 5-2."

What if that doesn't happen? Welcome to the make-or-break moment for the Longhorns in 2026 and the potential fallout if Texas suffers that third loss.

'Arch can play better': Will Texas QB answer?

Sarkisian stirred up a quarterback controversy of sorts – even if he confirmed Manning remains the starter for the Week 8 matchup against Ole Miss. Sarkisian confirmed quarterback KJ Lacey will get first-team reps in practice . Will that be any different than previous weeks?

"Not to me but we'll see how the week goes," Sarkisian said.

This is a moment for Manning, however. The redshirt junior quarterback remains the most-talked about QB in college football the last two seasons. To be clear, there was no way Manning would meet the hype and expectations heaped on the nephew of NFL legends Peyton and Eli Manning — the latter who starred with the Rebels from 1999-2003.

"Arch can play better for us," Sarkisian said. "He's our starter, but I need to see a better version of Arch Manning like I need to see a better version of a lot of guys on our offensive football team right now."

"I haven't put good film on tape the past five weeks," Manning said . "I'm going to be better. I'm going to better for myself, I'm going to better my teammates and I'm going to better for my coaches.

What is wrong with Arch? Defenses are taking the deep ball away, which is the strength in Manning's game. Manning had 13 TDs and three interceptions on passes of 20 yards or more last season, according to PFF.com . This year, he has two TDs and three interceptions. In the last two weeks, Manning is 3 of 8 for 145 yards with one TD and one interception on passes of 20 yards or more.

Manning also is 17 of 29 (58.6%) for 181 yards one TD and one interception when not being blitzed – an average of 6.2 yards per attempt that has knocked the explosives out of the passing attack.

"I feel like I'm being too hesitant to be honest, I'm going to die on the hill of I'm letting it rip," Manning said.

How important is this start? Win, and all that noise dies down like it did after the 24-23 victory against No. 1 Ohio State on Sept. 12 . Struggle and lose, and the rep count for Lacey will be a talking point and the rumors of Manning either entering the transfer portal or the 2027 NFL Draft will continue to swell. How has Manning responded after a meeting with Sarkisian this week?

"He has a chip on his shoulder and I appreciated it," Sarkisian said.

Can Steve Sarkisian turn two-loss Texas around?

Sarkisian pointed to the reasons for the shocking 27-24 loss to Florida in Week 7. The Longhorns had just 19 total offensive plays in the second half. Sarkisian lamented a "crummy call" on a rollout pass with Manning and pointed to the parity in the SEC. After all, Florida beat Ole Miss 52-28 on Sept. 26.

"The biggest area where I was disappointed — and I think we all were and all are — we just were really poor in critical situations in the game," Sarkisian said.

That tends to fall on coaching. Sarkisian does deserve credit for back-to-back College Football Playoff appearances in 2023-24. Texas has a 39-10 record since 2023 – the sixth-best record among Power 4 schools behind Ohio State (43-7), Georgia (42-7), Oregon (42-7), Notre Dame (40-8) and Ole Miss (39-8).

The Longhorns are tied with the Buckeyes and Bulldogs for most NFL Draft picks the last three years at 29.

But this year was supposed to be different. The Athletic reported Texas spends between $45-55 million on NIL — and Manning, edge rusher Colin Simmons, tackle Trevor Goosby and receiver Cam Coleman are expected to be first-round picks in the 2027 NFL Draft .

A third loss would make the College Football Playoff a long-shot for the third straight season, and Sarkisian would take heat for under-performing with a loaded roster. Would it be time to hand someone else the keys to the Lamborghini ?

The hot-seat talk would heat up exponentially for Sarkisian, and the question at hand is simple.

Sarkisian had back-to-back five-star quarterbacks in Quinn Ewers and Manning. The Longhorns have played for a SEC championship and reached the College Football Playoff semifinals in that stretch. But Texas is 7-9 against top-10 teams and 3-7 against top-five teams under Sarkisian.

As if that's not enough, Simmons — a Sporting News Midseason All-American who leads the FBS with 10.5 sacks — is expected to miss a few weeks with a high ankle sprain . This is the latest setback for the Longhorns, who have had drama attached to most of their games this season.

In Week 2, it was the fallout from the postgame interview with Holly Rowe. Simmons was penalized for "simulating using the restroom" during a 20-17 victory against Tennessee on Sept. 26, and the fallout from the back-to-back losses to Oklahoma and Florida still stands.

"You deal with things every year," Sarkisian said. "Some are more public than others, but you deal with stuff every year but you manage them accordingly as they come."

Now, the soap-opera season continues against the Rebels, and a trip to No. 18 LSU is still on the schedule for Nov. 18. Can Texas silence the noise in prime time?

articles.title: A Q&A on the state of NIL: College agents open up about negotiations, transfer decisions, more
articles.summary: Get a peek inside the world of NIL via interviews with multiple active agents.
articles.body:
The modern era of college football recruiting is -- in some ways -- the wild west. Thanks to NIL, revenue sharing and players being able to enter the transfer portal, it has become one of the most chaotic parts of the sport.

One of the people tasked with helping players navigate it all are name, image and likeness agents. In addition to a wide variety of other responsibility, agents help players broker NIL deals, choose which school is best for them and help them maximize their market value.

The Sporting News spoke with a couple of NIL agents in Charles Cox of Red Envelope Sports and Peter Webb of QB Reps to learn more about how the industry works and about what being an NIL agent means.

Red Envelope represents several NFL, college and high school athletes, including New Orleans Saints receiver Devaughn Vele and Washington State quarterback Caden Pinnick. QB Reps, which only signs quarterbacks, features clients in USC's Jayden Maiava, Wake Forest's Gio Lopez, Vanderbilt's Jared Curtis and Tennessee's George MacIntyre as well as Los Angeles Rams rookie Ty Simpson and Denver's Bo Nix in the NFL.

Below, both Cox and Webb discuss a number of topics, from who they negotiate with at the schools to how transfer decisions are made. MORE: Here are college football's 30 highest paid players

TSN: How long have you been in the business and how did you get involved in the business?

Charles Cox: "A longtime friend Don Yee, he's represented Tom Brady since Tom came out of Michigan, still represents Tom. He represents three NFL head coaches [Jim Harbaugh, Sean Payton and Mike McCarthy]. Don had heard I had sold my company and he had rebranded his NFL agency to Red Envelope Sports about five years ago, and wanted someone to take it over.

Long story short, [I] ended up buying the agency from him. I took over the NFL agency. We started the NIL division about two years ago. [We] just tried to approach it in the same way we approached our NFL side of the business in a boutique-like way, offering families senior agent experience."

Peter Webb: "I've been a sports agent for 22 years. I've never done anything else in my career since graduating law school, and worked with professional athletes in a lot of different sports. I always recruited at the college level and represented them as professional athletes. Five years ago, instead of recruiting them when they're sophomores or juniors in college, we started recruiting when they were in high school. So it's not like my job changed, to be honest. We just started recruiting them earlier."

TSN: What does the process of finding a player a fit and matching that with compensation work?

Webb: " When a kid is trying to pick a school, we're talking to Michigan, we're talking to Notre Dame, we're talking to Florida. We're helping them understand what that all looks like. Not just necessarily their financial package, because we really try to stay away from that.

We're concentrating on the school, the location, their community, their track record, their coaching staff, the quarterbacks that have come through that, their process, like their recruiting class, the development, like we're looking at a lot, a lot of different things. The financial package for us, we try to make that come in after they've already selected the school they're going to."

Cox: "We try to focus on generating the best football outcome for the player, and if you do that, the money is highly correlated with that if you go find the best spot. In this day and age, you try to focus on head coach security, right? Because you don't want to put a young man into a program where he could have to be there for six or 12 months and have to leave immediately. Which is hard, right? Because the coaches leave just as much as the players."

Webb: "Every year when we are dealing with the top programs in the country, I already can tell a kid 'hey, if your final five are LSU, Bama, Tennessee, Georgia, and Miami, I already have a really good idea what it's going to look like for all these schools, they're all going to be competitive. So just go pick the best school for you, and then I'll make it work.'"

Cox: "Obviously, the player has to build a great relationship with the position coach because that's who they're going to spend the vast majority of their time with, right? So all those things when you huddle up with a family and and try to figure out." MORE: How Michigan's Bryce Underwood is failing to live up to massive NIL deal

TSN: Who are you typically communicating with at schools? Is it general managers, coaches or both?

Cox: "When you're dealing with NIL, FBS, Power-Four schools, the Group of Six schools, virtually everyone has a general manager. And if it's not a general manager on paper, it's kind of a de facto GM."

Webb: " I'm talking to the head coaches. I'm talking to offensive coordinators, and I'm talking to the quarterback coaches as well as their GM and recruiting coordinator, director of player personnel."

Cox: "I never call coaches, that isn't my thing. I think they're a little bit out of the loop on the money. That's got to be frustrating for them, that they're kind of taken out of the money piece. I don't know if they don't like dealing with agents or they're kind of just annoyed by the dynamic of them being left out of such an important piece of the puzzle."

TSN: December is a chaotic time, as the Early Signing Period coincides with the coaching carousel and the College Football Playoff. What is it like navigating that?

Cox: " I've got a very transactional background, so it's not crazy to me. It's a blast. Solving problems with a gun to your head, that's fun to me. It's going to be crazy for the coaches and the staff because they aren't classically trained in this. These guys are classically trained in other things.

They have God-given abilities to communicate and train these kids and inspire them on the field that they're not good at this stuff, right? That doesn't make them bad coaches or bad professionals, they're being asked to do things they have no track record in. This is human resources."

Webb: "A lot goes into the portal because sometimes kids don't want to transfer, but they get recruited from other schools and other coaches. 'hey, come here, making promises—come here, you'll play right away. We can get you on the field. Using that angle of playing time can be very attractive. That's that's one. The second part is sometimes you have boosters and donors and collectives, calling and offering extremely, you know, lucrative financial package to come somewhere else and play."

Cox: " How the portal is structured with now 10 days in the first week of January, much of [that] crosses over with some of the FBS schools starting school. It's ridiculous that the concept of GMS and agents speaking is somehow looked down upon by the industry. It'd be ridiculous to ask these young men to go find a new place, negotiate their deal, and fly around on official visits in 10 days, yeah, and then enroll in a new school without professional help." MORE: Who are college football's highest paid head coaches?

TSN: What are conversations like for players wanting to enter the transfer portal or stay put?

Cox: " We play that role of insurance agent. That if things go bad at the last minute, when a school tells you, 'Hey, I think you should find a new place to play—which they do, by the way—right at the end of the semester, or something changes at the last minute in November, before signing day. We can go create opportunities out of thin air because we're always in the mix with all these FBS schools."

Webb: "Our job is really to say 'look, if you take the money out of it, what is the best scenario for you to develop and get on the field?' Because if your dream is to play in the NFL, then what's the best way to do that? Sometimes it's not just getting up and leaving and transferring to a new school right away for playing time."

Cox: " We're really the most important to the client when things don't go their way. When things go their way, then we're able to, you know, generate, you know, leverage for them and and just put a little bit of fear into the school that 'this young man has options.' He's not stuck with you."

Webb: "We're very big on, just because you're not playing your first year doesn't mean you hit the portal and chase something and start over again. I think that separates us too, is trying to make sure that our kids understand that you need to be developed. You need to give yourself a chance to learn the system, to learn the offense, to build your relationships with coaches. And it's hard if you are changing every year."

TSN: What would you say to players who want to represent themselves or avoid having an agent?

Cox: "I feel very strongly that we will be able to get more money for you, Mr. Player and his family, than you will be able to get for yourself.

I don't care who you are. I don't care if you're a CEO of a Fortune 100 company, or you're a freshman, you know, college football player, representing yourself with respect to money and employment is very difficult, right? It's awkward, it gets emotional, and if it doesn't go perfectly, you know, you're starting the relationship off on a bad foot."

Webb: " Take a five-star quarterback who goes to a college, and let's say he's getting a million dollars. $100,000 out a million dollars might be from rev-share, which means $900,000—90% of his money—is going to come through endorsement deals. It's going to come through multimedia rights partners.

So that kid then has to work with the school and fulfill tons of obligations for the school providing these endorsement services. So does a dad or a mom or a kid want to have a phone call every week discussing the soft drink deal, the automobile deal, the insurance deal, the banking deal, the apparel deal? They're all part of his package. 'Hey, you have this shoot. You got to do this social media post. You have this appearance.'"

TSN: What are some of the biggest misconceptions about what you do?

Webb: " People in the industry think, 'Why are these agents taking commissions off of deals that the kids are getting while they're in college, they should get that money anyway.' For quarterbacks and skill guys, it's just completely inaccurate. To make up the money that the school's paying them. There are a lot of obligations and deliverables that they have to fulfill, and having an agent to make sure that this deal for this brand is good for you. This deal is not good for you. This deal takes too much time. This isn't fair market value. So just because a school says, 'Hey, we want you to do this Pepsi deal, and we're going to give you $25,000, you need an agent to say, 'That deal is actually worth $125,000. Here's why.'"

Cox: " There's different kinds of programs, that are evolving from, this program used to be a program that developed young players, and now because of the economics, just can't justify developing young players. We've heard FBS programs say, 'I'm not recruiting high school players anymore. I'm just doing portal and Junior College.

And you understand why because these coaches are being asked to do a lot. They're being asked to coach a position, they're being asked to recruit. They're being asked to manage a team. They're being asked to now deal with the portal, which is hundreds and hundreds of names and extra work and review. So, you kind of have to use your time wisely, and not to mention the overall pressure of only having three to five,years to build something."

TSN: Describe some of the biggest challenges about your job.

Webb: "When kids get to school, other schools recruiting them through coaches, collectives and street guys trying to recruit them to switch schools to hit the portal because it's not for their the kids' best interest.

Our job is to serve the kids' best interest, and a lot of people that are recruiting our quarterbacks to flip or to transfer or whatever it is, they're not doing it for the kid's best interest."

Cox: " The most challenging parts revolve around the parents usually. Their expectations are out of whack with reality or they don't quite understand how much work is involved on our end. Sometimes the clients who are raised very well find it very difficult to do the "smart football business" things you need to do in order to prepare for changed circumstances out of their control like visiting other schools while they're committed to a school, etc."

TSN: What are some of the most rewarding parts of the job?

Cox: " Typically when you have a client who may not have been an elite recruit in high school and you help them make the right moves, whether that be to FCS or JUCO in their first one to two years that allows them to develop on and off the field and achieve their dreams at playing at a higher level at a bigger school for their last two to three years of college. Obviously, seeing a college player you've had a long-term relationship with make the NFL is an awesome feeling as well."

Webb: " For me there was a lot of reward signing Ty Simpson in high school. Being a part of that process to Alabama, and then that whole why he waited, he sat, he developed. He didn't take the easy road, he didn't go transfer for millions of dollars. He continued to put his head down and grind and trust the process. That got him on the field, and he was a first-round pick.

Those are the most rewarding things for me to see kids go through adversity, but stick it out and trust the process. And I think that's kind of what our agency is kind of founded on: Don't run when adversity hits you, don't chase the money. What's going to give you the best chance for success for the long term?"

TSN: What changes do you think could be made to improve the NIL Agent industry or what would you like to see added?

Cox: " I don't think you get to a solution without coming up with some hybrid student-athlete employee classification for everyone, so they can collectively bargain. And they can create some parameters that that actually you know include the voice of the student athletes themselves."

Webb: "Number one is there's got to be agent certification. That's number one. That's one of the biggest problems is that you have runners and street guys and coaches doing multi-million-dollar deals for kids with zero experience, zero background, zero resume. They're not registered in the state. They're not registered with the school. They're not registered. There's no compliance checks."

articles.title: Arch Manning transfer rumors: LSU, Ole Miss, Oregon among top options if Texas QB leaves in 2027
articles.summary: A look at where Arch Manning could end up if he decides to enter the transfer portal after this season.
articles.body:
What was supposed to be Arch Manning's dream season at Texas has gone poorly. The Longhorns didn't even make it to the end of October before getting two losses, and Manning has not played well.

Even Longhorns head coach Steve Sarkisian said after Texas' loss to Florida that he was going to give an uptick to Manning's backup, KJ Lacey. Although a benching of Manning appears unlikely, it is not entirely out of the realm of possibility.

Thanks to how poorly his season has gone, there is speculation that he may forgo the 2027 NFL Draft and choose to stay in college for another season. While the expectation is that he will remain at Texas if he does stay, let's take a look at some of the best landing spots for Manning if he does decide to enter the transfer portal.

Arch Manning top transfer portal destinations

Manning played high school football for four seasons in Louisiana, playing out of Isidore Newman in New Orleans. His high school sits just 82 miles southeast of Baton Rouge, and Manning was born and grew up in Louisiana.

If Manning wants to hone in on his development as a quarterback, LSU head coach Lane Kiffin has an impressive track record in doing so. He made Jaxson Dart into a first-round NFL Draft pick, and helped discover Trinidad Chambliss from DII Ferris State, who is expected to be a top signal-caller picked for 2027.

Sam Leavitt hasn't played great so far this season, and although Kiffin won't admit it, he was the coach's fourth transfer choice behind Trinidad Chambliss, Brandon Sorsby and Washington's Demond Williams.

What better way to start fresh for Manning than to return to his roots and play under an offensive mind like Kiffin?

Georgia head coach Kirby Smart has historically stuck with quarterbacks he has recruited out of high school and developed in Athens. Speaking of, Smart and the Bulldogs were one of three finalists for Manning coming out of high school.

But Smart has also landed some transfer portal quarterbacks as backups to Gunner Stockton, including Oregon transfer Bryson Beaver this year, and adding Jaden Rashada in 2024.

Stockton is a fifth-year senior this season, and his backup, Ryan Puglisi has completed 36 passes for 413 yards with three touchdowns and two interceptions his last two seasons. Getting a quarterback with real game experience like Manning might not be a bad idea for Smart, even if that's non-traditional for him.

If Ole Miss head coach Pete Golding wants another way to beat Kiffin aside from his team's 32-24 victory earlier this season, look no further. Golding already successfully prevented Chambliss from leaving Ole Miss and joining Kiffin at LSU. How about doing it a second time in a row by getting Manning to come to Oxford?

Chambliss is going to the NFL after this season. It would also be incredibly cool to see Manning go where his grandfather, Archie, and uncle Eli played. That's not a bad recruiting pitch if you're Golding, either. In Oxford, Manning might have to compete for the starting job with current backup Deuce Knight, who transferred in from Auburn this offseason. But his game experience might give him an edge.

Oregon head coach Dan Lanning has had an unexpectedly down year at quarterback this season. Starter Dante Moore is expected to miss a second consecutive game as he left the game against UCLA on Oct. 10 with a concussion.

In his absence, he's shuffled between Dylan Raiola and Brock Thomas, although neither of them have played all too great. Lanning has yet to name a starter between the two ahead of Oregon's game against Illinois this week, although Raiola appears to have an edge .

Moore is expected to go to the NFL in 2027, and Raiola is a junior this season. The quarterback room is pretty wide open behind Raiola for next season. Although Oregon might be far from home for Manning, Lanning has a solid track record at transfer portal quarterbacks as Moore came in from UCLA, and Dillon Gabriel transferred in from Oklahoma in 2024.

Indiana and Miami might make sense if Manning improves

At this point, I think Indiana and Miami only really make sense for Manning on paper. While both teams have cashed in on landing some big-time transfer portal quarterbacks, such as Cam Ward and Carson Beck at Miami and Fernando Mendoza and Josh Hoover at Indiana.

But I think for both schools to be interested in Manning, he will have to play a lot better than he has been. Beck and Hoover both had multiple seasons with over 3,000 yards passing, and had consistent success as a starter across multiple seasons. Mendoza had thrown for 4,712 with 30 touchdowns over two years with Cal.

While Manning's stats are slightly similar, I don't think he's put enough good games on tape to where he'd be an attractive option for either school. Across his two seasons, he has 20 turnovers, and has not played well in his five losses to Ohio State, Florida and Georgia last season and vs. Oklahoma and Florida so far this year. Indiana and Miami will be likely to pursue a quarterback that's played much more consistent. But if Manning has a strong back half of the season, both schools could absolutely be in play.

articles.title: Patrick Mahomes’ $362,000 luxury watch is just one detail in the Chiefs quarterback’s $86.8 million financial story
articles.summary: Patrick Mahomes wore a $362,000 Hublot to Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's wedding, and people noticed.
articles.body: Patrick Mahomes wore a $362,000 Hublot to Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's wedding, and people noticed. The price tag still looks small next to his paycheck. The Chiefs quarterback is credited with $86.8 million in total earnings. Football accounts for $56.8 million of that. The other $30 million comes from memorabilia, licensing and brand partnerships. His contract extension, reworked to $504.75 million through 2033, drives the first number, while deals like the one with Hublot feed the second. The watch is the flashy part of the story, not the biggest part.A $362,000 watch inside an $86.8 million incomeThe watch is a Hublot MP-10 Tourbillon Weight Energy System, limited to 50 pieces, according to reports from the wedding weekend. Brittany Mahomes wore a $100,000 lab-grown diamond necklace, so the couple's outfits turned into a quick price comparison. Patrick's wrist won.It was not a one-off flex. Mahomes has been a Hublot ambassador since September. The brand contacted his agents in November 2024, and the campaign shoot took place in Kansas City in May 2025. CEO Julien Tornare keeps a personalised autograph jersey from Mahomes in a glass case in his office. "The biggest thing is just doing stuff you're really invested in," Mahomes said. He has also said he saw a link between the uniqueness of his game and the Hublot brand.Hublot sells watches from $6,400 to $575,000, so the MP-10 sits near the top of the range but not at the peak. The terms of his deal are not public. Still, ambassador work like this fits the kind of income inside that $30 million off-field figure.His taste goes back further. Alex Smith, his mentor in Kansas City, introduced him to high-end watches. A 2023 estimate put his collection above $852,000, and his Rolex Daytona Rainbow alone retails for close to $450,000.How the contract drives his football incomePatrick Mahomes signed a 10-year, $450 million extension in July 2020. It has since been reworked to a total of $504.75 million, running through the 2033 season. That deal is the base of the $56.8 million on-field number.Scale helps here. The watch is about 0.4 percent of his $86.8 million. His $30 million in off-field income would cover more than 80 of them. His football pay would cover roughly 157.The off-field money is split across memorabilia, licensing and corporate partnerships. Signed items and licensing deals keep earning even when he is not on the field, which makes that $30 million steadier than it looks.The pull is easy to explain. He was MVP of Super Bowl LVIII, finishing 34 of 46 for 333 yards, and watch fans were already tracking his wrist that night. Brands pay for access to a quarterback who keeps winning, and the Chiefs pay him for the same reason.The contract runs to 2033. The watch will be old news long before then.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

However, effort doesn't change the fact that Washington is sitting at 1-4-1 and just lost star wide receiver Terry McLaurin to a season-ending knee injury. Getting the season back on track will be a challenge.

If the Commanders are open to trading players, possibly for receiver help, Daron Payne is a strong candidate. The 29-year-old defensive tackle has started all six games this season, has recorded 14 tackles, and will interest teams seeking defensive-line help.

Payne is also in a contract year and carrying a cap hit of $28 million.

Potential Suitors: Chicago Bears , Jacksonville Jaguars

Payne is in his 9th season in the NFL, and all of it with Washington. He's been a valuable, reliable player on the defensive front, but he carries a big cap hit. In fact, it's the largest on the entire roster, followed by Sam Cosmi at just over $20 million. He's also a free agent at the end of the season, and Washington hasn't seemed inclined to extend him.

Over his career, Payne has recorded 446 tackles (242 solo), 38 sacks, eight forced fumbles, six fumble recoveries, one interception, 25 pass defenses, and 50.5 stuffs. Missing two games in 2025 was only the second time he's missed that many games in a season, with the first coming in 2019.

It will be interesting to see if the Commanders are willing to trade away the face of their defensive front.
